nameStory: The Pink-footed Goose gets its charming name from its distinctively colored feet and legs, which range from bright pink to orange-pink. The scientific name tells the same story - 'brachyrhynchus' comes from ancient Greek meaning 'short bill,' referring to this goose's notably compact beak compared to other grey geese.
description: The Pink-footed Goose is a medium-sized grey goose that's actually quite rare to spot in New England, being far from its usual range. These Arctic breeders are about the size of a Canada Goose, with brownish-grey plumage, a dark head and neck, and that telltale pink bill with a dark tip. They're built for long migrations, with strong wings and a streamlined body that carries them thousands of miles between their Greenland and Iceland breeding grounds and their European wintering areas.

idTips.label: Pink feet and legs
idTips.description: Bright pink to orange-pink feet and legs that stand out against muddy ground or water - much more vibrant than the duller feet of most other geese

idTips.label: Pink and black bill
idTips.description: Short, compact bill that's pink at the base with a distinct black tip - feels stubby compared to other geese if you could touch it

idTips.label: Dark head contrast
idTips.description: Dark brown head and neck that contrasts sharply with the lighter grey-brown body, creating a two-toned appearance

idTips.label: Grey-brown body
idTips.description: Overall greyish-brown plumage with subtle barring that gives a textured, layered look rather than solid coloring

idTips.label: Size and build
idTips.description: Compact, medium-sized goose with a shorter neck than Canada Geese, giving it a more rounded, sturdy appearance

habitat: In New England, Pink-footed Geese are extremely rare vagrants that might occasionally appear in coastal areas, large lakes, or agricultural fields where other migrating geese congregate. They prefer open water near mudflats or short-grass areas for feeding, similar to where you'd find Canada Geese or other waterfowl during migration.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare vagrant possibility during spring migration in March-May, most likely mixed in with flocks of Canada Geese or other migrating waterfowl.
seasonality.summer: Not expected in New England during summer as they breed in the high Arctic regions of Greenland and Iceland.
seasonality.fall: Best chance for a rare sighting during fall migration from September-November when birds might be blown off course from their normal European migration route.
seasonality.winter: Possible but very unlikely vagrant in winter months, as most birds winter in Europe rather than North America.

funFact: Pink-footed Geese are incredible navigators that can fly non-stop for over 1,800 miles from Iceland to Scotland, using magnetic fields and star patterns to find the exact same wintering spots their parents used - which makes their rare appearances in New England all the more remarkable!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Greater White-fronted Goose, but Pink-footed Geese lack the white forehead patch and have much pinker (not orange-yellow) feet. Remember: 'Pink feet = Pink-footed' - if the feet aren't obviously pink, it's probably something else.
contextualKnowledge: Pink-footed Geese are nicknamed 'pinkfeet' by birdwatchers and are considered a major vagrant rarity in New England - any sighting would be significant enough to alert local birding communities and should be carefully documented with photos.
compareHints: Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives. They're also much darker overall than Snow Geese and have that distinctively short, stubby bill that sets them apart from other Anser species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips.
Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese.
Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill.
Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose.
